title: The Error You Get Before It Runs: constexpr, and What the Compiler Refuses to Compute

questions.question: Lesson 02-09 found that a struct member read before it was written produces no warning on gcc or clang and runs clean under the address sanitizer. What happens to the same read inside a constant expression?
options: It is folded to zero, since the compiler must pick some value
It compiles, and the sanitizer catches it as before
It is a warning, which -Werror can turn into an error
Both compilers refuse to compile it, because undefined behaviour is not a constant expression
questions.explanation: At runtime the compiler may assume undefined behaviour does not happen. In a constant expression it has to produce the value, and there is none to produce. That makes it the one place this bug is caught for free, with no tool and no flag.

questions.question: constexpr on a function means what, exactly?
options: That it is inlined at every call site
That it has no side effects and can be reordered freely
Instruction: every call is evaluated during translation
Permission: it may be evaluated during translation if used where a constant is required, and otherwise runs like any function
questions.explanation: The same function runs happily at runtime on a value the compiler does not know. To require compile-time evaluation you use the result where only a constant will do: a constexpr variable, a static_assert, an array bound or a template argument.

questions.question: const int size = readings.size(); int buffer[size]; is refused. Why, when const int kCount = 8; int buffer[kCount]; is accepted?
options: Because size is a std::size_t and array bounds must be int
const says nobody may change it, not that the value is known at build time; the second works only because an integral const initialised by a constant expression is itself usable as one
Because readings.size() might return zero
Both are refused; C++ has no variable-length arrays at all
questions.explanation: That C++98 rule covers integral types only, which is why the same thing with a const double fails on both compilers. The feature appears to work until the first time it matters.

questions.question: The lesson's suite checks the table's values with RC_CHECK at runtime rather than with static_assert. Why, given that static_assert is the stronger check?
options: static_assert cannot compare array elements
To keep compile times down on the Windows lane
A static_assert on the answer would mean an unfinished exercise could not be built, and a suite that cannot run tells a learner nothing about which function to write
Because the values are not actually known at compile time
questions.explanation: The compile-time property is proven separately, by constexpr variables at file scope that compile only if the compiler could work the values out. Proving when an evaluation happened and checking what it produced are two different jobs.

questions.question: The first version of the lesson's benchmark reported 0.0 us for both the table and the loop at -O2, and the test failed. What had happened?
options: The accumulated total was never used, so the optimiser deleted both loops; a volatile store fixed it
steady_clock has microsecond granularity, so short work rounds to zero
The table was so fast that both fell below the timer resolution
constexpr evaluation had already computed both answers at compile time
questions.explanation: The guard that was supposed to keep the work, if (total < 0) std::cout << "";, reads like it does and does not. A benchmark whose result nothing reads is a way of timing an empty loop.

questions.question: Can a test prove that a given expression was NOT evaluated at compile time?
options: Yes, by comparing the binary size with and without the constexpr keyword
Yes, with std::is_constant_evaluated in C++17
No. You can prove one happened, by putting it where a runtime value would be refused, and there is no portable way to assert the compiler declined to fold something
Yes, by timing the first call against later ones
questions.explanation: So compile-time evaluation is not a property to check in a test. It is a property to require in the declaration, by making the variable constexpr, so a build that could not do the work fails.
